title: Queensland targets union misconduct with new bill
full_text:
The Queensland government has announced sweeping industrial relations reforms in a bid to stamp out union violence and misconduct, including a new “fit and proper” person test for officials seeking worksite access.
During parliament on Wednesday, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie tabled the Crisafulli government’s review of the state workers’ compensation scheme and industrial relations laws, along with its response.
The review, launched earlier this year, was led by former Bleijie-appointed WorkCover chair Glenn Ferguson and Industrial Relations Commissioner Gary Black.
In total it made 104 recommendations, 75 of which the government accepted in full, a further 14 agreed to in principle, six having been noted, and nine not accepted, Mr Bleijie said. The government was due to introduce the bill on Wednesday night.
Outlining the government’s response to the review, Mr Bleijie told parliament the reforms – which include the introduction of a fit and proper test for union officials seeking right of entry powers on worksites – would bring Queensland in to line with other states. They would also “begin to shift the balance back on Queenslanders’ favour”, he said.
“We have agreed, for example, to introduce a robust, fit and proper person test for union officials seeking to gain lawful right of entry powers on work sites, drawing a line in the sand for the unacceptable and threatening behaviour that has been allowed to run rampant on Queensland work sites under Labor,” Mr Bleijie said.
“Queenslanders expect and deserve an industrial relations system that works for them, ensuring they both feel safe at their workplace, are paid competitively, and that we have productive workplaces.
“These reforms are about fairness, productivity, resolving industrial relations issues in an efficient way that supports workers, and provides essential services for Queensland.”
The bill is also expected to include more “freedom” around who can represent workers in industrial disputes and wage negotiations, and increased maximum penalties for WorkCover fraud.
It also changes the test for psychological injuries so employment must be the “major significant contributing factor” rather than “a significant contributing factor”.
Queensland Council of Unions general secretary Jacqueline King said the changes would make it harder for frontline workers – such as paramedics, police and nurses – to access support.
“Psychological injuries can have more than one cause. A worker’s job can significantly contribute even when other factors also play a part,” Ms King said. “Requiring work to be the major contributing factor risks shutting workers out of compensation and access to the support they need.
“These changes should not be rushed through.”
Accusing the Labor opposition of manipulating industrial relations and workplace health and safety “to benefit their CFMEU mates” when in government, Mr Bleijie said the government was “determined to turn around the culture of violence and intimidation” within the state’s construction sector.
An ongoing commission of inquiry is probing claims of CFMEU misconduct in Queensland. The inquiry, which was recently extended, has previously heard that construction bosses and workers, and government bureaucrats were threatened and intimidated by members of the militant union.
It has also been told that joint state-federal funded infrastructure projects, including Cross River Rail and Centenary Bridge upgrade, were delayed and made more expensive by CFMEU industrial action.
Mr Bleijie said the reforms would help to protect the state’s workers compensation scheme, and save small and family businesses more than $1.46bn a year in increased premiums.
“Through this review and the implementation of the recommendations, this government is demonstrating its determination to deliver a modern, productive, and fair industrial relations and workers’ compensation scheme,” he said, adding that, without the reforms, it was estimated premiums would surge 26 per cent over the next five years.
